The **United States women's national soccer team** (**USWNT**), designated as **USA** by [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA"), represents the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") in international [women's soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_soccer "Women's soccer"). The team is governed by the [United States Soccer Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Soccer_Federation "United States Soccer Federation") and competes in [CONCACAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF "CONCACAF"), the FIFA confederation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean. The U.S. team is the most successful team in international women's soccer, winning four [Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "FIFA Women's World Cup") titles ([1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1991 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup"), and [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup")), five [Olympic gold medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Football at the Summer Olympics") ([1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), and [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament")), nine [CONCACAF W Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF_W_Championship "CONCACAF W Championship") titles, and one [CONCACAF W Gold Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF_W_Gold_Cup "CONCACAF W Gold Cup") title. It has medaled in every Women's World Cup and Olympic women's soccer tournament except for the [2016 Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") tournament and the [2023 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup"); on both occasions, the U.S. was eliminated by [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden_women's_national_football_team "Sweden women's national football team") after a [penalty shootout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_\(association_football\) "Penalty shoot-out \(association football\)") in the first round of the knockout stage.
After mostly being ranked No. 2 from 2003 to 2008 in the [FIFA Women's World Rankings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Rankings "FIFA Women's World Rankings"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-rank-3) the team was ranked No. 1 continuously from March 2008 to November 2014, the longest consecutive top ranking of any team.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-4) Since FIFA rankings were established in 2003, the team has been ranked No. 1 for a total of 13 years; the team with the next-longest tenure, [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team"), has been ranked No. 1 for a total of 41⁄2 years. The USWNT has never been ranked lower than fifth in the world.
The team was selected as the [U.S. Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee")'s Team of the Year in 1997 and 1999,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-5) and _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ chose the entire team as the 1999 Sportswomen of the Year for its traditional [Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsman_of_the_Year "Sportsman of the Year") honor.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-6) On April 5, 2017, USWNT players and the U.S. Soccer Federation reached a new [collective bargaining agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining_agreement "Collective bargaining agreement") that would, among other things, lead to a pay increase for players.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-7) In February 2022, numerous current and former players of the USWNT settled a lawsuit with U.S. Soccer for $24 million and a requirement that male and female soccer players be paid equally, regardless of the proportion of prize money they receive; this was the first instance of this standard in the world.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-nbcequality-8) FIFA still distributes significantly more funds to its member associations for the men's event.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-9)
The United States will be a co-host of the [2031 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2031_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2031 FIFA Women's World Cup"), and the USWNT will earn automatic entry as a result.
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
Main article: [History of the United States women's national soccer team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "History of the United States women's national soccer team")
### Origins
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins")]
The passing of [Title IX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Title_IX "Title IX") in 1972, which outlawed gender-based discrimination for federally-funded education programs, spurred the creation of women's [college soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_soccer "College soccer") teams across the United States at a time when women's soccer was rising in popularity globally.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-10) In its first foray into women's international soccer, the U.S. Soccer Federation asked coach [Mike Ryan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ryan_\(soccer_coach\) "Mike Ryan \(soccer coach\)") to select a roster of collegiate players to participate in the 1985 [Mundialito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mundialito_\(women\) "Mundialito \(women\)") tournament in Italy.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-11) The team played its [first match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "1985 United States women's national soccer team") on August 18, 1985, losing 1–0 to [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_women's_national_football_team "Italy women's national football team"), and finished the tournament in fourth place.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Wahl-2019-13)
[University of North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_soccer "North Carolina Tar Heels women's soccer") coach [Anson Dorrance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anson_Dorrance "Anson Dorrance") was hired as the team's first full-time head coach in 1986 with the goal of fielding a competitive women's team at the next Mundialito and at future tournaments.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Wahl-2019-13) In their first Mundialito under Dorrance, the United States defeated [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_women's_national_football_team "China women's national football team"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team"), and [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team") before finishing as runners-up to Italy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-14) Dorrance gave national team appearances to teenage players, including future stars [Mia Hamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Hamm "Mia Hamm"), [Julie Foudy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Foudy "Julie Foudy"), and [Kristine Lilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristine_Lilly "Kristine Lilly"), instead of the college players preferred by the federation.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-15) The U.S. played in the [1988 FIFA Women's Invitation Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_FIFA_Women's_Invitation_Tournament "1988 FIFA Women's Invitation Tournament") in China, a competition meant to test the feasibility of a regular women's championship. The U.S. lost in the quarterfinals to eventual champions [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_women's_national_football_team "Norway women's national football team").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Wahl-2019-13)
### 1990s: First World Cup and Olympic wins
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1990s: First World Cup and Olympic wins")]
Following the 1988 tournament, FIFA announced plans for a new women's tournament, named the [1st FIFA World Championship for Women's Football for the M&M's Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1991 FIFA Women's World Cup") until it was retroactively named the "World Cup". The U.S. qualified for the tournament by winning the [inaugural CONCACAF Women's Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "1991 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), hosted by Haiti in April 1991. The U.S. outscored its opponents 49–0 for the confederation's sole World Cup berth.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Wahl-2019-13)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-16) The team played several exhibition matches against European opponents to prepare for the World Cup; its players quit their regular jobs to train full-time for meager compensation.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-18) Dorrance utilized a 4–3–3 formation that was spearheaded by the "[Triple-Edged Sword](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-Edged_Sword "Triple-Edged Sword")" of forward [Michelle Akers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Akers "Michelle Akers") and wingers [Carin Jennings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carin_Jennings "Carin Jennings") and [April Heinrichs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_Heinrichs "April Heinrichs").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-19)
At the World Cup, the U.S. won all three of its group stage matches and outscored its opponents 11–2.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-11-20) The Americans achieved a 7–0 victory in the quarterfinals over [Chinese Taipei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Taipei_women's_national_football_team "Chinese Taipei women's national football team"), fueled by a five-goal performance by Akers in the first 50 minutes of the match.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-11-20) In the semifinal against [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team"), Jennings scored a [hat-trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat-trick_\(association_football\) "Hat-trick \(association football\)") in the first half as the U.S. won 5–2.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-21) The team's lopsided victories in the earlier rounds had brought attention from American media outlets, but the final match was not televised live in the U.S.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-11-20) The United States won the inaugural Women's World Cup title by defeating [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_women's_national_football_team "Norway women's national football team") 2–1 in the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "1991 FIFA Women's World Cup final"), played in front of 65,000 spectators at [Tianhe Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tianhe_Stadium "Tianhe Stadium") in [Guangzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou"). Both goals were scored by Akers, who finished as the top goalscorer of the tournament, with ten goals.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-22) Jennings was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-23)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Lilly356.jpg/250px-Lilly356.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lilly356.jpg)[Kristine Lilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristine_Lilly "Kristine Lilly") (left) and [Mia Hamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Hamm "Mia Hamm")
Despite its World Cup victory, the U.S. team remained in relative obscurity and received only a small welcome from several U.S. Soccer Federation officials upon arrival at [John F. Kennedy International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy_International_Airport "John F. Kennedy International Airport") in New York City.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-24) The team was given fewer resources and little attention as the federation focused on improving the [men's national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_men's_national_soccer_team "United States men's national soccer team") in preparation for the [1994 men's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_FIFA_World_Cup "1994 FIFA World Cup") that would be hosted in the United States.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-23-25) The women's team was placed on hiatus after the 1991 World Cup, only playing twice in 1992. They returned the following year to play in several tournaments hosted in [Cyprus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus "Cyprus"), Canada, and the United States, and won a second [CONCACAF Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "1993 CONCACAF Women's Championship") title.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-23-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-26)
The U.S. played in several tournaments to prepare for the [1995 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1995 FIFA Women's World Cup") and its qualification campaign. The first was the [inaugural Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_Algarve_Cup "1994 Algarve Cup") in Portugal, which saw the team lose 1–0 to Norway in the final. The Algarve Cup was followed by a victory at the [Chiquita Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiquita_Cup?action=edit&redlink=1 "Chiquita Cup \(page does not exist\)"), an exhibition tournament hosted on the U.S. East Coast against Germany, China, and Norway.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Litterer-1994-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-28) Dorrance resigned from his position as head coach in August 1994 and was replaced by his assistant, [Tony DiCicco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_DiCicco "Tony DiCicco"), a former professional goalkeeper who played in the [American Soccer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Soccer_League_\(1933%E2%80%9383\) "American Soccer League \(1933–83\)").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Lisi-23-25)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-29) Under DiCicco, the USWNT secured a berth at the 1995 World Cup by winning the [1994 CONCACAF Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "1994 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), during which they scored 36 goals and conceded only one.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-Litterer-1994-27)
In February 1995, the U.S. women's program opened a permanent training and treatment facility in [Sanford, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanford,_Florida "Sanford, Florida"), and began a series of warm-up [friendlies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friendlies "Friendlies") that were paid for by [Nike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nike,_Inc. "Nike, Inc.").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-30) The team topped their group in the Women's World Cup, despite a 3–3 tie with China in the opening match and losing goalkeeper [Briana Scurry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Briana_Scurry "Briana Scurry") to a [red card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_card_\(association_football\) "Red card \(association football\)") in their second match. The U.S. proceeded to defeat Japan 4–0 in the quarterfinals, then lost 1–0 to Norway in the semifinals. The team finished in third place by achieving a 2–0 victory over China.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] At the [inaugural Olympic women's soccer tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") during the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), the U.S. won the gold medal, defeating China 2–1 in the final.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-31)
On July 10, 1999, a stadium of 90,000 people—the largest-ever audience for a women's sporting event at the time—watched the United States play China in the final of the [1999 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup") in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-32) After a back-and-forth game, the score was tied 0–0 at full-time, and remained so after [extra time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra_time_\(association_football\) "Extra time \(association football\)"), leading to a [penalty shootout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_\(association_football\) "Penalty shoot-out \(association football\)"). [Brandi Chastain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brandi_Chastain "Brandi Chastain") scored the final kick for the United States, winning the game and the World Cup. She dropped to her knees, whipped off her jersey, and celebrated in her [sports bra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_bra "Sports bra"), an image which made the cover of _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ and the front pages of newspapers around the world.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-33) The U.S. victory brought significant media attention to women's soccer and women's sports in general, and inspired many girls to play soccer.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-34) In the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"), the USWNT were close to defending their gold medal but were controversially defeated by Norway in the final with a golden goal in extra time, which involved an alleged handball in the lead-up.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-35)
### 2000s: two Olympic gold medals
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2000s: two Olympic gold medals")]
[![A soccer game between the United States and Canada, seen from behind one of the goals](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/Wambach_2003.jpg/250px-Wambach_2003.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wambach_2003.jpg)[Abby Wambach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Wambach "Abby Wambach") plays off a corner kick at the [2003 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2003 FIFA Women's World Cup") bronze medal game against Canada
In the [2003 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2003 FIFA Women's World Cup"), the U.S. defeated Norway 1–0 in the quarterfinals but lost 3–0 to Germany in the semifinals. The team then defeated Canada 3–1 to claim third place.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-36) [Abby Wambach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Wambach "Abby Wambach") was the team's top scorer with three goals, while [Joy Fawcett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joy_Fawcett "Joy Fawcett") and [Shannon Boxx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Boxx "Shannon Boxx") made the tournament's all-star team. In the [2004 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), the last major international tournament for Hamm and Foudy, the U.S. earned the gold medal, winning 2–1 over Brazil in the final on an extra time goal by Wambach.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-37)
At the [2007 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2007 FIFA Women's World Cup"), the U.S. defeated England 3–0 in the quarterfinals but then suffered its most lopsided loss in team history when it lost to Brazil 4–0 in the semifinals.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-38) The U.S. recovered to defeat Norway to take third place.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-39) Wambach was the team's leading scorer with 6 goals, and Lilly was the only American named to the tournament's all-star team.
The team won another gold medal in the 2008 Olympics,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-40) but interest in the Women's National Team had diminished since their performance in the 1999 World Cup. However, the second women's professional league was created in March 2009, [Women's Professional Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Professional_Soccer "Women's Professional Soccer").
### 2010s: Olympic and then World Cup triumphs
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2010s: Olympic and then World Cup triumphs")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Jogadoras_dos_Estados_Unidos_no_momento_da_cobran%C3%A7a_dos_p%C3%AAnaltis_%28DSC01176%29.jpg/250px-Jogadoras_dos_Estados_Unidos_no_momento_da_cobran%C3%A7a_dos_p%C3%AAnaltis_%28DSC01176%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jogadoras_dos_Estados_Unidos_no_momento_da_cobran%C3%A7a_dos_p%C3%AAnaltis_\(DSC01176\).jpg)The USWNT at the [2011 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup")
In the quarterfinal of the [2011 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup") in Germany, the U.S. defeated [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_soccer_team "Brazil women's national soccer team") 5–3 on penalty kicks. Wambach's goal in the 122nd minute to tie the game 2–2 has been voted the greatest goal in U.S. soccer history and the greatest goal in Women's World Cup history.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-ESPN-41)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-42) The U.S. then beat France 3–1 in the semifinal, but lost to Japan 3–1 on penalty kicks in the Final after drawing 1–1 in regulation and 2–2 in [overtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_\(sports\) "Overtime \(sports\)"). [Hope Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Solo "Hope Solo") was named the tournament's best goalkeeper and Wambach won the silver ball as the tournament's second-best player.
In the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 2012 Summer Olympics"), the U.S. won the gold medal for the fourth time in five Olympics by defeating Japan 2–1 in front of 80,203 fans at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium"), a record for a women's soccer game at the Olympics.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-43) The United States advanced to face Japan for the gold medal by winning the semifinal against Canada, a 4–3 victory at the end of extra time.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-USWNTOlympics2012-44) The 2012 London Olympics marked the first time the USWNT won every game en route to the gold medal and set an Olympic women's team record of 16 goals scored.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-USWNTOlympics2012-44)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Womens_World_Cup_parade_July_2015.JPG/250px-Womens_World_Cup_parade_July_2015.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Womens_World_Cup_parade_July_2015.JPG)A [ticker tape parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker_tape_parade "Ticker tape parade") in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan") celebrating the team's [2015 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") victory
The [National Women's Soccer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Soccer_League "National Women's Soccer League") started in 2013, and provided competitive games as well as opportunities to players on the fringes of the squad.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-46) The U.S. had a 43-game unbeaten streak that spanned two years – the streak began with a 4–0 win over Sweden in the [2012 Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Algarve_Cup "2012 Algarve Cup"), and came to an end after a 1–0 loss against Sweden in the [2014 Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Algarve_Cup "2014 Algarve Cup").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-48)
The U.S. defeated Japan 5–2 in the [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup final") of the [2015 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup"), becoming the first team in history to win three Women's World Cup titles. In the 16th minute, [Carli Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carli_Lloyd "Carli Lloyd") achieved the fastest [hat-trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat-trick "Hat-trick") from kick-off in World Cup history, and Wambach was greeted with a standing ovation for her last World Cup match.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-49) Following their 2015 World Cup win, the team was honored with a [ticker tape parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker_tape_parade "Ticker tape parade") in New York City, the first for a women's sports team, and honored by President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-50) On December 16, 2015, however, a 1–0 loss to China in Wambach's last game meant the team's first home loss since 2004, ending their 104-game home unbeaten streak.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-51)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Alex_morgan_2016.jpg/250px-Alex_morgan_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alex_morgan_2016.jpg)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Estados_Unidos_x_Su%C3%A9cia_-_Futebol_feminino_-_Olimp%C3%ADada_Rio_2016_%2828861417721%29.jpg/250px-Estados_Unidos_x_Su%C3%A9cia_-_Futebol_feminino_-_Olimp%C3%ADada_Rio_2016_%2828861417721%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Estados_Unidos_x_Su%C3%A9cia_-_Futebol_feminino_-_Olimp%C3%ADada_Rio_2016_\(28861417721\).jpg)
[Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") being challenged by [Hikari Takagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hikari_Takagi "Hikari Takagi") (15) during a match against Japan in Cleveland on June 5, 2016, and again, being challenged by [Nilla Fischer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilla_Fischer "Nilla Fischer") (5) during a match against Sweden in [Brasília](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bras%C3%ADlia "Brasília") on August 12, 2016.
In the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), the U.S. drew against [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden_women's_national_football_team "Sweden women's national football team") in the quarterfinal; in the following penalty kick phase, Sweden won the game 4–3. The loss marked the first time that the USWNT did not advance to the gold medal game of the Olympics, and the first time that the USWNT failed to advance to the semifinal round of a major tournament.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-52)
After the defeat in the 2016 Olympics, the USWNT underwent a year of experimentation which saw them losing three home games. If not for a comeback win against Brazil, the USWNT was on the brink of losing four home games in one year, a low never before seen by the USWNT. 2017 saw the USWNT play 12 games against teams ranked in the top-15 in the world.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-53)
Throughout 2018, the U.S. would pick up two major tournament wins, winning both the [SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SheBelieves_Cup "SheBelieves Cup")[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-SheBelieves-54) and the [Tournament of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tournament_of_Nations "Tournament of Nations").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-55) The team would enter qualifying for the [2019 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup") on a 21-game unbeaten streak and dominated the competition, winning all five of its games and the tournament whilst qualifying for the World Cup as well as scoring 18 goals and conceding none.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-56) On March 7, 2018, Alyssa Alhadeff, the captain of the Parkland Soccer Club, who was killed by gunman [Nikolas Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolas_Cruz "Nikolas Cruz") in the [Parkland High School shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkland_High_School_shooting "Parkland High School shooting") nearly three weeks earlier, was honored by the U.S. prior to a game against [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_women's_national_football_team "England women's national football team") in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida") during the [2018 SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_SheBelieves_Cup "2018 SheBelieves Cup"). Alhadeff's teammates and family were invited to the game and presented with official jerseys that featured her name.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-57) The U.S. won the game 1–0, winning its second SheBelieves Cup title in three years.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-SheBelieves-54) On November 8, 2018, the U.S. earned their 500th victory in team history after a 1–0 victory over [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_women's_national_football_team "Portugal women's national football team").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-58) The start of 2019 saw the U.S. lose an away game to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_women's_national_football_team "France women's national football team"), 3–1, marking the end of a 28-game unbeaten streak and their first loss since a 1–0 defeat to [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_soccer_team "Australia women's national soccer team") in July 2017.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-59)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Demanding_Equity_%2848274759786%29.jpg/250px-Demanding_Equity_%2848274759786%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Demanding_Equity_\(48274759786\).jpg)USWNT at a parade in their honor after the 2019 Championship
The USWNT started off their [2019 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup") campaign with a [13–0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v_Thailand_\(2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup\) "United States v Thailand \(2019 FIFA Women's World Cup\)") victory against [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand_women's_national_football_team "Thailand women's national football team"), setting a new Women's World Cup goal record. [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") equaled Akers' record of scoring five goals in a single World Cup match, while four of her teammates scored their first World Cup goals in their debut at the tournament.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-60) The U.S. would win its next match against [Chile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chile_women's_national_football_team "Chile women's national football team") 3–0[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-61) before concluding the group stage with a win of 2–0 over Sweden.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-62) The team emerged as the winners of [Group F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Group_F "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup Group F") and would go on to face [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_women's_national_football_team "Spain women's national football team") in the Round of 16, whom they would defeat 2–1 thanks to a pair of [Megan Rapinoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe "Megan Rapinoe") [penalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_kick_\(association_football\) "Penalty kick \(association football\)").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-63) The team would achieve identical results in their next two games. With 2–1 victories over [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_women's_national_football_team "France women's national football team")[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-64) and then [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_women's_national_football_team "England women's national football team")[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-65) seeing them advance to a record third straight [World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup final"), they played against the Netherlands for the title. They beat the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_women's_national_football_team "Netherlands women's national football team") 2–0 in the final on July 7, 2019, becoming the first team in history to win four Women's World Cup titles.
On July 30, 2019, [Jill Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jill_Ellis "Jill Ellis") announced that she would step down as head coach following the conclusion of the team's post-[World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup") victory tour on October 6, 2019.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-66)
[Vlatko Andonovski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlatko_Andonovski "Vlatko Andonovski") was hired as head coach of the USWNT in October 2019, replacing Ellis.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-67)
### 2020s: fifth Olympic gold
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2020s: fifth Olympic gold")]
The USWNT began the new decade by winning both the [2020 CONCACAF Women's Olympic Qualifying tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_CONCACAF_Women's_Olympic_Qualifying_Championship "2020 CONCACAF Women's Olympic Qualifying Championship") (which qualified the team for the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics")) and the [2020 SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_SheBelieves_Cup "2020 SheBelieves Cup") titles.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-conca2020-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-69)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-SBC20-70)
In early March 2020, due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the USSF canceled previously scheduled USWNT friendlies against [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_soccer_team "Australia women's national soccer team") and [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-71) Later that same month, it was announced by the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) and the Tokyo Metropolitan Government that the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics") were to be postponed until July 2021.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-72) The USWNT played their first game in eight months on November 27, 2020, when they took on the [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_women's_national_football_team "Netherlands women's national football team") in a friendly match. [Rose Lavelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Lavelle "Rose Lavelle") and [Kristie Mewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristie_Mewis "Kristie Mewis") scored, the team winning the game 2–0.
On July 21, 2021, the USWNT lost 3–0 against Sweden in the opening round of group stage at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), thus ending a 44-match unbeaten streak.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-73) The U.S. rebounded by winning their 2nd match against [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_football_team "New Zealand women's national football team"), before concluding the group stage by drawing 0–0 with Australia. The team finished second in the group stage and qualified for the knockout stage. They first faced World Cup runners-up [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_women's_national_football_team "Netherlands women's national football team"), with whom they drew 2–2 after extra-time before winning the match in a penalty shootout. The USWNT advanced to the semifinals, where they faced [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_women's_national_soccer_team "Canada women's national soccer team"). However, the team lost to Canada 1–0 by a penalty scored by [Jessie Fleming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessie_Fleming "Jessie Fleming"). They later faced Australia again in the bronze medal match in a rematch of their final group stage game. The U.S. won 4–3, making it the first time the team had won the bronze medal.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-74)
In July 2022, the team competed in the [CONCACAF W Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_CONCACAF_W_Championship "2022 CONCACAF W Championship"). The USWNT won its group, outscoring opponents 9–0 in the group stage, and then won the semifinal 3–0 against Costa Rica and the final 1–0 against Canada.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-75)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-76)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-78) It was their ninth CONCACAF championship title and earned automatic berths for the [2023 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup"), the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics") in France, and the [2024 CONCACAF W Gold Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_CONCACAF_W_Gold_Cup "2024 CONCACAF W Gold Cup").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-80)
In November 2022, the USWNT's 71-game home unbeaten streak ended, after a 2–1 defeat in an exhibition game against [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-81)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Chaos_during_USWNT_v_Germany_Paris_2024.png/250px-Chaos_during_USWNT_v_Germany_Paris_2024.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Chaos_during_USWNT_v_Germany_Paris_2024.png)Chaos in the USWNT's defense at the 2024 Olympics.
At the [2023 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup"), the USWNT were in [Group E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Group_E "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup Group E") along with Netherlands, Portugal and Vietnam. They had gone in hoping to be the first men's or women's team to pull off a [three-peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-peat "Three-peat") at the World Cup.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-82) The USWNT opened with a 3–0 win over Vietnam, followed this up with a 1–1 draw against Netherlands and finished up with a 0–0 draw against Portugal, to finish second in the group, avoiding elimination after a shot from Portugal struck the goalpost in injury time. This marked the fewest points the team has ever gained in a group stage (they won at least two group games in every other tournament including 1991 when only two points were awarded for a win) and set them up for a round of 16 match against Sweden, where they played out a goalless draw and lost 5–4 after a penalty shootout. This marked the first time since the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") that the United States did not reach the semifinals of a major tournament.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-83) It also marked the first Women's World Cup the United States would not finish in the Top 3, and their earliest elimination in either the Women's World Cup or the Olympics. On August 17, 2023, Andonovski resigned as head coach and [Twila Kilgore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twila_Kilgore "Twila Kilgore") became the interim head coach.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-84) That August the team dropped to third in the FIFA Women's World Ranking, their worst ever position.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-85)
The USWNT qualified for the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics") by winning the [2022 CONCACAF W Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_CONCACAF_W_Championship "2022 CONCACAF W Championship"). This would be the first tournament since the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") to not feature [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") as she was not selected for the roster. 
They were placed in Group B with [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia_women's_national_football_team "Zambia women's national football team"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team"), and [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_soccer_team "Australia women's national soccer team"). They won all three group-stage games by scores of 3–0, 4–1, and 2–1, respectively.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-86)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-88) In the knockout rounds, they defeated Japan 1–0 in extra time and then Germany in the semifinal, also 1–0 in extra time.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-89)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-90) Commentators expressed concern that because of the two extra-time games in a tournament with a compressed schedule, the USWNT would be more fatigued than their opponent in the final, Brazil, who had beaten both of their knockout-round opponents in regulation time.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-91) However, they prevailed 1–0 in the final to win the gold medal, their first since 2012 and fifth overall.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-92) Ten of their twelve goals in the tournament were scored by the self-named "Triple Espresso" attackers [Trinity Rodman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Rodman "Trinity Rodman"), [Mallory Swanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallory_Swanson "Mallory Swanson"), and [Sophia Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia_Smith_\(soccer,_born_2000\) "Sophia Smith \(soccer, born 2000\)").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-93)

### Media coverage
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Media coverage")]
U.S. television coverage for the five Women's World Cups from 1995 to 2011 was provided by [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN")/ABC and [Univision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Univision "Univision"),[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-si2014-12-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-95) while coverage rights for the three Women's World Cups from 2015 to 2023 were awarded to [Fox Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports "Fox Sports") and [Telemundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telemundo "Telemundo").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-96)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-97) In December 2021, a deal was signed to broadcast TV coverage of other USWNT games between [TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_\(American_TV_network\) "TNT \(American TV network\)") and [TBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TBS_\(American_TV_channel\) "TBS \(American TV channel\)") and streaming on [HBO Max](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO_Max "HBO Max") through the end of 2030. The USWNT games in the [2014 CONCACAF Women's Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "2014 CONCACAF Women's Championship") and the [2015 Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Algarve_Cup "2015 Algarve Cup") were broadcast by Fox Sports.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-99) [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Sports "NBC Sports") will broadcast the [Olympic tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Football at the Summer Olympics") through [2032](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2032_Summer_Olympics "2032 Summer Olympics").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-100)
The [1999 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup") [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup final") set the original record for largest U.S. television audience for a women's soccer match, averaging 18 million viewers.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-102) It was the most viewed English-language U.S. broadcast of any soccer match until the [2015 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup final") between the United States and Japan.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-103)
The 2015 Women's World Cup Final between the United States and Japan was the most watched soccer match, men's or women's, in American broadcast history.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-npr.org-104) It averaged 23 million viewers and higher ratings than the NBA finals and the Stanley Cup finals.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-npr.org-104)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-105) The final was also the most watched US-Spanish language broadcast of a FIFA Women's World Cup match in history.
Overall, there were over 750 million viewers for the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup, making it the most watched Women's World Cup in history. The FIFA Women's World Cup is now the second-most watched FIFA tournament, with only the men's FIFA World Cup attracting more viewership.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-106)
### In popular culture
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: In popular culture")]
A narrative nonfiction book covering the entire history of the team from 1985 to 2019 called _The National Team: The Inside Story of the Women Who Changed Soccer_ was named one of _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity_Fair_\(magazine\) "Vanity Fair \(magazine\)")'_s best books of 2019 and made [NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR")'s 2019 year-end books list.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-107)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-108) A book about the team's 1999 Women's World Cup campaign, _Girls of Summer: The U.S. Women's Soccer Team and How It Changed the World_ was released in 2001 and in 2020 Netflix announced a film based on the book.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-109) In 2023, Netflix released a four-episode documentary series titled _Under Pressure: The U.S. Women's World Cup Team_ which followed the team's progress at the 2023 Women's World Cup.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-110)
In 2005, [HBO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HBO "HBO") released a documentary called _[Dare to Dream: The Story of the U.S. Women's Soccer Team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dare_to_Dream:_The_Story_of_the_U.S._Women's_Soccer_Team "Dare to Dream: The Story of the U.S. Women's Soccer Team")_.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-111) In 2013, a documentary about the [1999 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup")-winning team called _The 99ers_ was produced by former player [Julie Foudy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julie_Foudy "Julie Foudy") and [ESPN Films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_Films "ESPN Films").[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-112)
### Attendance
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Attendance")]
The [1999 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup") [final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup final"), in which the United States defeated China, set a world attendance record for a women's soccer event of 90,185 in a sellout at the [Rose Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rose_Bowl_\(stadium\) "Rose Bowl \(stadium\)") in Southern California (until it was broken on March 30, 2022, with 91,553 people at the Camp Nou in Barcelona, Spain in the second-leg of a UEFA Women's Champions League match).[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-113) The record for Olympic women's soccer attendance was set by the 2012 Olympic final between the USWNT and Japan, with 80,023 spectators at Wembley Stadium.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-114) The USWNT's attendance record for a home friendly (50,644) was set on April 6, 2024, in a 2–1 [SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SheBelieves_Cup "SheBelieves Cup") win over [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team") at [Mercedes-Benz Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercedes-Benz_Stadium "Mercedes-Benz Stadium") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta").[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-115)
## Legal issues
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Legal issues")]
### Pay discrimination
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Pay discrimination")]
Since 2016, the players of the U.S. team had waged an escalating [legal fight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._women's_national_soccer_team_pay_discrimination_claim "U.S. women's national soccer team pay discrimination claim") with the [United States Soccer Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Soccer_Federation "United States Soccer Federation") (USSF) over [gender discrimination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender_inequality_in_the_United_States "Gender inequality in the United States"). Central to their demands was equal pay. The players pointed to their lower paychecks as compared to their [male counterparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_men's_national_soccer_team "United States men's national soccer team") despite their higher record of success in recent years.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-116)
In April 2016, five U.S. team players filed a wage-discrimination action against the USSF with the [Equal Employment Opportunity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission "Equal Employment Opportunity Commission").[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-117) The group consisted of [Hope Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Solo "Hope Solo"), [Carli Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carli_Lloyd "Carli Lloyd"), [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan"), [Megan Rapinoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe "Megan Rapinoe"), and [Becky Sauerbrunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Becky_Sauerbrunn "Becky Sauerbrunn").
One year later, in April 2017, the U.S. team agreed to a new [collective bargaining agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collective_bargaining_agreement "Collective bargaining agreement") (CBA) with the USSF. The agreement stated that the U.S. team players would have an increased base pay and improved match bonuses. These changes could increase their previous pay from $200,000 to $300,000. However, the CBA did not guarantee equal pay compared to the men's team. The CBA's five-year term through 2021 ensured that the next negotiation would not become an issue for the team for the 2019 World Cup and the 2020 Olympics. On top of this CBA, the USSF had agreed to pay the players for two years' worth of unequal [per-diem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_diem#United_States "Per diem") payments.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-118)
On March 8, 2019, 28 members of the U.S. team filed a gender discrimination lawsuit against the USSF.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-119) The lawsuit, filed in the [U.S. District Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_Central_District_of_California "United States District Court for the Central District of California") in Los Angeles, accused the USSF of "institutional gender discrimination."[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-120) The lawsuit claimed that the discrimination affected not only the amount the players were paid but also their playing, training, and travel conditions. In May 2020, several key parts of the case were dismissed, with federal judge [R. Gary Klausner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._Gary_Klausner "R. Gary Klausner") noting that the team had agreed to take higher base compensation and other benefits in their most recent CBA instead of the bonuses received by the men's team.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-121)
On March 8, 2021, the second anniversary of the team's [pay discrimination lawsuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._women's_national_soccer_team_pay_discrimination_claim "U.S. women's national soccer team pay discrimination claim"), Congresswomen [Doris Matsui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doris_Matsui "Doris Matsui") and [Rosa DeLauro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosa_DeLauro "Rosa DeLauro") introduced the Give Our Athletes Level Salaries (GOALS) Act to ensure the team members "are paid fair and equitable wages compared to the [U.S. Men's team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_men's_national_soccer_team "United States men's national soccer team")."[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-122) The GOALS Act threatened to cut federal funding for the [2026 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Cup "2026 World Cup") if the USSF did not comply.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-123)
On February 22, 2022, the USSF agreed to settle the lawsuit for $24 million, contingent upon the U.S. team agreeing to a new CBA. $22 million would go to the players named in the case, and $2 million would contribute toward players' post-playing career and other women's soccer charitable efforts.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-nbcequality-8)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-124) On May 18, 2022, the U.S. team agreed to a new CBA that would run through 2028 and would equalize compensation, bonuses, and other work conditions between the women's and the men's national teams friendlies, therefore finalizing the legal settlement. The new agreement mandates that men and women split prize money from international competitions equally, making it the first such instance in the world.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-125)
### Artificial turf
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Artificial turf")]
Along with their [lawsuit for pay-equity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._women's_national_soccer_team_pay_discrimination_claim "U.S. women's national soccer team pay discrimination claim"), the US Women's Soccer players have fought [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA") on policies regarding [artificial turf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_turf "Artificial turf"). This battle to eliminate its use in major women's games heightened around the [2015 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") in Canada; during this tournament, the US played eight of their ten games on artificial turf.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-126) Prior to the 2015 World Cup, [Abby Wambach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Wambach "Abby Wambach") headed a discrimination lawsuit with other global soccer stars including [Marta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marta_\(footballer\) "Marta \(footballer\)") of Brazil and [Homare Sawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homare_Sawa "Homare Sawa") of Japan.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-127) Due to the tournament's quick approach, the suit was dropped as players were denied an expedited hearing.

### Player records
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Player records")]
See also: [List of United States women's international soccer players](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_women's_international_soccer_players "List of United States women's international soccer players")      _As of October 13, 2026_ [[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-149)     _Players in**bold** are still active with the national team._
The women's national team boasts the first six players in the history of the game to have earned 200 [caps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_\(sport\) "Cap \(sport\)").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-150) These players have since been joined in the 200-cap club by several players from other national teams, as well as by seven more Americans: Kate Markgraf, Abby Wambach, Heather O'Reilly, Carli Lloyd, Hope Solo, Becky Sauerbrunn, and Alex Morgan.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team#cite_note-200_cap_club_2023-151) Kristine Lilly, Carli Lloyd, and Christie Pearce are three of the four players in international soccer to earn more than 300 caps, the other being [Canada's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_women's_national_soccer_team "Canada women's national soccer team") [Christine Sinclair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Sinclair "Christine Sinclair").
In March 2004, [Mia Hamm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mia_Hamm "Mia Hamm") and [Michelle Akers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michelle_Akers "Michelle Akers") were the only two women and the only two Americans named to the [FIFA 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_100 "FIFA 100"), a list of the 125 greatest living soccer players chosen by [Pelé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pel%C3%A9 "Pelé") as part of [FIFA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA "FIFA")'s centenary observances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Major competitions
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=United_States_women%27s_national_soccer_team&action=edit&section=42 "Edit section: Major competitions")]
  * **[World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "FIFA Women's World Cup")**

     _Champions (4):_ [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1991 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1999 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup")      _Runners-up:_ [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup")      _Third place (3):_ [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "1995 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [2003](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2003 FIFA Women's World Cup"), [2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2007 FIFA Women's World Cup")
  * **[Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Football at the Summer Olympics")**

     _Gold medalists (5):_ [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 1996 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"), [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament")      _Silver medalists:_ [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2000 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament")      _Bronze medalists:_ [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament")
  * **[CONCACAF W Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF_W_Championship "CONCACAF W Championship")**

     _Champions (9):_ [1991](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "1991 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_CONCACAF_Women's_Invitational_Tournament "1993 CONCACAF Women's Invitational Tournament"), [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "1994 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_CONCACAF_Women's_Gold_Cup "2000 CONCACAF Women's Gold Cup"), [2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_CONCACAF_Women's_Gold_Cup "2002 CONCACAF Women's Gold Cup"), [2006](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_CONCACAF_Women's_Gold_Cup "2006 CONCACAF Women's Gold Cup"), [2014](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "2014 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), [2018](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_CONCACAF_Women's_Championship "2018 CONCACAF Women's Championship"), [2022](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_CONCACAF_W_Championship "2022 CONCACAF W Championship")      _Third place:_ [2010](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_CONCACAF_Women's_World_Cup_Qualifying "2010 CONCACAF Women's World Cup Qualifying")
  * **[CONCACAF W Gold Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF_W_Gold_Cup "CONCACAF W Gold Cup")**

     _Champions:_ [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_CONCACAF_W_Gold_Cup "2024 CONCACAF W Gold Cup")
